summary: Discusses the applicability of the QUIC transport protocol, with a focus on caveats that affect application protocol development and deployment over QUIC. It is aimed at designers of application protocol mappings to QUIC and the implementers of those protocols. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If you are building something on QUIC, this is the advice sheet. It covers the surprises that can trip up people moving apps onto it.

subtitle: Practical guidance for building applications on top of QUIC

tldr.problem: QUIC is a powerful new transport protocol with advanced features like stream multiplexing, 0-RTT connection setup, and encryption built-in, but application developers need guidance on important caveats and design tradeoffs when using it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides detailed guidance on QUIC's capabilities and limitations across fifteen major areas: fallback strategies, 0-RTT replay risks, stream usage, packetization, error handling, connection migration, termination, and more.
tldr.outcome: Developers can build robust QUIC applications by understanding when fallback to TCP is needed, how to handle 0-RTT safely, how to use multiplexed streams effectively, and how to manage connection lifecycle and security concerns.

today: RFC 9308 is an Informational RFC providing guidance to application developers using or designing protocols for QUIC. It remains the definitive reference for understanding QUIC's applicability and constraints.

sections.title: QUIC and Its Applications
sections.content:
QUIC is a modern transport protocol that runs over UDP and integrates encryption (TLS 1.3) from the start. It supports multiple concurrent streams within a single connection, 0-round-trip-time (0-RTT) connection establishment, and connection migration when endpoints change addresses. HTTP/3, the latest version of HTTP, uses QUIC as its transport.

This RFC is aimed at application developers and protocol designers who want to use QUIC for their applications. It does not explain how QUIC works internally but rather highlights the practical considerations and potential gotchas that application designers must address. Understanding these caveats helps developers build reliable, performant, and secure applications on top of QUIC.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC is a better, faster way to send messages across the Internet. This document tells app designers what to watch out for so their apps work correctly and safely.

sections.title: Fallback and Network Compatibility
sections.content:
Although QUIC runs over UDP, measurements show that roughly 3–5% of networks block all UDP traffic. Applications using QUIC must be prepared to fall back to an alternative protocol (usually TLS over TCP for HTTP). However, fallback is not simple: downgrading to TCP exposes control information to network modification, and falling back to TLS versions older than 1.3 weakens encryption. TCP also lacks the stream multiplexing QUIC provides, so applications may need to implement multiplexing in the application layer.

Fallback must never silently weaken security or violate the application's expectation of confidentiality and integrity. If secure communication cannot be achieved, the connection should fail and inform the user, rather than degrade silently. The IETF Transport Services (TAPS) specifications provide guidance on managing fallback across multiple protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks block QUIC, so apps need a backup plan. But the backup cannot be less safe. If an app cannot use QUIC safely on a network, it should say so rather than secretly downgrading.

sections.title: Multiplexing with Streams
sections.content:
QUIC's stream multiplexing is one of its key features: an application can open multiple independent streams on a single connection, and data loss or latency on one stream does not block others (no head-of-line blocking). However, stream multiplexing is transparent to the network—the network cannot distinguish or prioritize streams—so applications requiring different network treatment should use separate QUIC connections.

When designing an application, developers should send data requiring specific ordering on the same stream, while data that can be processed independently should use separate streams. Streams can be unidirectional or bidirectional, initiated by either endpoint. The QUIC implementation should expose stream properties (who initiated it, whether it is bidirectional) rather than requiring applications to infer them from stream IDs. Applications must also consider the maximum number of streams allowed and manage this limit carefully to avoid deadlock.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC lets multiple messages travel at the same time without blocking each other. But the network does not know about the messages inside—it just sees the QUIC connection. So if you need different network treatment, you need different connections.

sections.title: 0-RTT Connection Setup and Replay Risk
sections.content:
QUIC supports 0-RTT (zero-round-trip-time) connection establishment, allowing applications to send data immediately on connection resumption, without waiting for the handshake to complete. This reduces latency but carries a risk: data sent in 0-RTT can be replayed by attackers, causing the server to process the same request multiple times.

Applications must carefully choose what data is safe to send in 0-RTT. Idempotent operations (those where repeating them has the same effect as doing them once) are generally safe. Other operations may need additional protections or profile definitions describing what can be safely resumed. HTTP provides explicit guidance on this. Applications can also adjust connection idle timeouts to manage the balance between keeping connections alive with PING frames and resuming idle connections using 0-RTT when appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC can skip some setup steps and go faster, but this lets attackers trick the server into doing the same thing twice. Apps must be careful about what they do in this fast mode.

sections.title: Error Handling and Termination
sections.content:
QUIC defines error handling at both transport and application layers. Transport errors (like protocol violations) terminate the entire connection via a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame. Applications define their own error code space, separate from QUIC's, and can signal stream-level errors (STOP_SENDING, RESET_STREAM) or connection-level errors.

QUIC provides three ways to terminate a connection: idle timeout (after an idle period with no activity), explicit immediate close (CONNECTION_CLOSE frame, which abruptly closes all streams), or stateless reset (when an endpoint has lost connection state). QUIC itself provides no graceful termination mechanism, so applications must implement this at the application layer if needed. Applications should be configurable for idle timeout values and should provide their own keep-alive mechanisms or explicitly manage session resumption after long idle periods.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, QUIC can close a connection. There are three ways to shut down: quietly timing out, slamming the door closed, or resetting. Apps need to handle these gracefully and decide when to close.

sections.title: Advanced Considerations
sections.content:
Several advanced considerations affect QUIC deployment. Connection Migration allows clients to change IP addresses while maintaining the connection (using the Connection ID), but path validation takes at least one round trip and resets congestion control. Packetization and Latency: applications cannot control how stream data is packed into packets; implementations may wait briefly to optimize bandwidth, potentially increasing latency. Applications requiring low latency should signal QUIC to flush packets immediately. Port Selection and Discovery: applications should use the same port for QUIC that they use for the TCP fallback protocol and register ALPN tokens for protocol negotiation.

Connection ID Management: servers should use non-zero-length connection IDs if clients might be behind NATs, enabling connection migration and load balancing. Quality of Service: applications should not multiplex flows needing different network treatment; instead, they should use separate QUIC connections. Version Negotiation: applications must decide how to handle different QUIC versions, which may have different behavior and features.
sections.plainLanguage: When building with QUIC, there are many details: addresses can change, packets can be delayed for efficiency, servers need unique IDs, and some apps need special treatment. All of these need careful thought.
